section.title: A catalog of essential functions
section.p: We can now build functions by formulas, graphs, tables, words, transformations, arithmetic, composition, and inverses. But calculus does not treat every function as a stranger.

Some families appear again and again. Lines describe constant rates. Polynomials describe smooth algebraic change. Rational functions show ratios and asymptotes. Trigonometric functions describe periodic motion. Exponential functions describe constant percentage change. Logarithms undo exponentials.
This catalog is not a list to memorize. It is a set of familiar shapes and stories.

subsection.title: Linear functions and units
subsection.p: The distance function for constant velocity had the form s(t)=s_0+vt. This is a linear function.
In general, a linear function has the form
The number m is the slope. It measures output change per unit input change:
The number b is the value at input 0: f(0)=b.

statement.p: Suppose a taxi ride costs 4 dollars to begin and 2.50 dollars per mile. If m is the number of miles, then
The slope is 2.50\frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{mile}}. The intercept is 4\text{ dollars}.
The units make the formula readable: 2.50\frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{mile}}\cdot m\text{ miles} = 2.50m\text{ dollars}.
A linear model says that equal changes in input produce equal changes in output.
The Celsius-to-Fahrenheit function is
The slope is \frac{9}{5}. This says that increasing the Celsius temperature by 1^\circ increases the Fahrenheit temperature by \frac{9}{5}^\circ.
The intercept is 32, because 0^\circ\text{ C}=32^\circ\text{ F}.
A linear function has constant average rate of change:
for every x_1\neq x_2.

subsection.p: Later, the derivative of a linear function will simply be its slope.

subsection.title: Powers and polynomials
subsection.p: Power functions have the form f(x)=x^p. The most familiar powers are x, x^2, x^3, x^4. They already appeared in the first chapter through finite differences. Squares grew with odd-number differences. Cubes grew faster.
Power functions describe scaling.

statement.p: The area of a circle of radius r is A(r)=\pi r^2. If the radius doubles, the area becomes A(2r)=\pi(2r)^2=4\pi r^2=4A(r). So doubling length multiplies area by 4.
The volume of a sphere of radius r is V(r)=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3. If the radius doubles, the volume becomes V(2r)=\frac{4}{3}\pi(2r)^3=8V(r). So doubling length multiplies volume by 8.
This is the basic difference between square growth and cubic growth.
For f(x)=Cx^p, multiplying the input by k multiplies the output by k^p:

subsection.p: A polynomial is a finite sum of power functions with nonnegative integer powers:
Here the coefficients a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n are real numbers, and a_n\neq 0. The number n is the degree of the polynomial.

Polynomials are defined for all real inputs. Their domains are \mathbb{R}. Their graphs have no breaks, holes, or vertical asymptotes. They may turn, cross the axis, or flatten, but they do not suddenly jump.

paragraphs.title: Leading behavior
paragraphs.p: Far from the origin, the highest-power term usually dominates the shape. For
the term 2x^5 eventually becomes much larger in size than -10x^2 and 3. So for large positive or negative x, the graph behaves roughly like y=2x^5.
This idea will become more precise when we study limits at infinity.

subsection.title: Rational functions and asymptotic behavior
subsection.p: A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials:
The denominator cannot be zero. Thus the natural domain is \{x\in\mathbb{R}:q(x)\neq 0\}.

example.title: Forbidden inputs of a rational function

statement.p: The function r(x)=\frac{x+1}{x^2-4} is undefined when x^2-4=0. Since x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2), the forbidden inputs are x=2 and x=-2.
So the natural domain is (-\infty,-2)\cup(-2,2)\cup(2,\infty).

subsection.p: Rational functions often show behavior that polynomials do not: vertical asymptotes, horizontal asymptotes, and holes.

statement.p: Suppose producing x items costs C(x)=100+5x dollars. The first 100 dollars is a fixed setup cost. The 5x dollars is the variable cost.
The average cost per item is
As x grows, the term \frac{100}{x} gets smaller. The average cost approaches 5 dollars per item. The line y=5 is a horizontal asymptote.

figure.caption: The average cost approaches the variable cost per item as the fixed cost is spread over more items.

paragraphs.title: Vertical asymptotes
paragraphs.p: The function f(x)=\frac{1}{x-2} is undefined at x=2. As x gets close to 2, the denominator gets close to 0, and the quotient grows very large in size. The vertical line x=2 is a vertical asymptote.
We will define this precisely with limits. For now, the important picture is this: a rational function can grow without bound near a forbidden input.

paragraphs.title: A hole instead of an asymptote
paragraphs.p: Not every forbidden input creates an asymptote. Consider h(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}. The input x=1 is forbidden, but for x\neq 1, h(x)=x+1. So the graph is the line y=x+1 with a hole at the missing point (1,2).
This is why domain restrictions matter. The formula simplifies, but the missing input remains missing.

subsection.title: Algebraic functions
subsection.p: Algebraic functions are built from polynomials using a finite number of algebraic operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and roots. Examples include \sqrt{x}, \sqrt{4-x^2}, \frac{\sqrt{x+1}}{x-3}, and \sqrt[3]{x^2+1}.
These functions often come from geometry.

statement.p: The circle of radius 2 centered at the origin satisfies x^2+y^2=4. Solving for y, we get y=\pm\sqrt{4-x^2}.
The upper half is f(x)=\sqrt{4-x^2}. The square root requires 4-x^2\ge 0, so -2\le x\le 2. The natural domain is [-2,2] and the range is [0,2].

paragraphs.title: A root changes smoothness
paragraphs.p: The function f(x)=\sqrt{x} has domain [0,\infty). Its graph starts at (0,0) and rises slowly after an initially steep beginning. Later, when we study derivatives, we will see that the tangent near x=0 is very different from the tangent of a polynomial.
So algebraic functions can be continuous and natural while still having behavior that needs care.

subsection.title: Trigonometric functions in radians
subsection.p: Motion can repeat. A wheel turns. A pendulum swings. A tide rises and falls. A point on a spring oscillates. The basic functions for periodic motion are sine and cosine.
On the unit circle, an angle \theta determines a point (\cos\theta,\sin\theta). The cosine is the horizontal coordinate. The sine is the vertical coordinate.

figure.caption: On the unit circle, cosine and sine are coordinates of the point reached by angle \theta.

subsection.p: The angle must be measured in radians for calculus. A radian is defined by arc length:

On the unit circle, the radius is 1, so the radian measure of an angle equals the length of the arc it cuts off. A full turn has circumference 2\pi, so a full turn is 2\pi radians. A half turn is \pi radians, and a quarter turn is \frac{\pi}{2} radians.

subsection.p: The sine and cosine functions have domain \mathbb{R} and range [-1,1]. They repeat every 2\pi:
The tangent function is \tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}. It has vertical asymptotes at x=\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi, k\in\mathbb{Z}.

example.title: Amplitude and period of sinusoidal motion

statement.p: A point moving up and down with height y(t)=3\sin(2t) has amplitude 3, because the output ranges from -3 to 3.
The factor 2 inside the sine makes the motion repeat faster than \sin t. Since sine repeats when its input increases by 2\pi, we need 2t to increase by 2\pi, so t increases by \pi. The period is \pi.

subsection.title: Exponential functions
subsection.p: Linear functions add the same amount for each equal step. Exponential functions multiply by the same factor for each equal step.

statement.p: A function of the form f(x)=a^x, where a\gt 0 and a\neq 1, is an exponential function.
If a\gt 1, the function grows. If 0\lt a\lt 1, the function decays.
Suppose a bacterial population doubles every 3 hours. If the initial population is P_0, then after t hours a natural model is
Check the doubling property: P(t+3)=P_0\,2^{(t+3)/3}=P_0\,2^{t/3+1}=2P_0\,2^{t/3}=2P(t).
Every time t increases by 3, the output doubles.
Suppose a radioactive substance loses half its mass every 8 days. If the initial mass is M_0, then
Then M(t+8)=\frac{1}{2}M(t). Every 8 days, the mass is cut in half.
For f(x)=a^x,
For a fixed step h, the output is multiplied by the same factor a^h, no matter where the step begins.

subsection.p: The domain of a^x is \mathbb{R} and the range is (0,\infty). Exponential functions never output 0 or a negative number.

One exponential function will become especially important in calculus: e^x, where e\approx 2.71828. Later we will earn its special role: e^x is the exponential function whose rate of change equals itself.

subsection.title: Logarithms as inverse functions
subsection.p: Since a^x is one-to-one for a\gt 0, a\neq 1, it has an inverse. That inverse is the logarithm base a.

statement.p: For a\gt 0, a\neq 1, \log_a x=y means a^y=x.
In words, \log_a x is the exponent needed on a to get x.

subsection.p: The logarithm has domain (0,\infty) and range \mathbb{R}. This is the reverse of the exponential function.

figure.caption: Exponential and logarithm functions are inverses, so their graphs reflect across the line y=x.

subsection.p: Because logarithms undo exponentials, \log_a(a^x)=x for all real x, and a^{\log_a x}=x for all x\gt 0.
The exponential laws become logarithm laws:

paragraphs.title: Natural logarithm
paragraphs.p: The logarithm base e is called the natural logarithm: \ln x = \log_e x. It satisfies \ln(e^x)=x and e^{\ln x}=x for x\gt 0.

subsection.title: The catalog at a glance
subsection.p: This table is not a substitute for understanding the shapes. It is a map. When a problem mentions constant rate, think linear. When it mentions repeated percentage change, think exponential. When it mentions periodic motion, think trigonometric. When it mentions undoing an exponential, think logarithm.

A function family is a first guess, not a proof. The next step is modeling: choosing a function because units, data, and behavior suggest it. That will be our last preparation before limits turn near into a precise mathematical tool.
